entry.title: Anduril and Qualcomm Announce BlueChip US-Made Laptop Line for Defense and Government
entry.content:
Links: bloomberg.com | source

Defense tech startup Anduril Industries and chipmaker Qualcomm have unveiled BlueChip, a new line of laptops designed and assembled in the United States for government and military use. The first-generation rugged laptops will be powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Series processors, with preorders scheduled to open in 2027.

The initiative aims to rebuild domestic computer manufacturing and secure the supply chain by sourcing roughly 90% of the device's components from the US or allied countries. The collaboration addresses growing concerns over reliance on overseas manufacturing for critical technology hardware used in defense sectors.

entry.title: Stanford Professors File Copyright Lawsuit Against Anthropic Over Claude Training
entry.content:
Links: stanforddaily.com | source | hacker news

Stanford professors Tobias Wolff and Chang-rae Lee are among a group of authors who opted out of the $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic copyright class-action settlement to file a separate lawsuit, Cruz v. Anthropic. The new complaint alleges that Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated copyrighted works from shadow libraries to train its Claude artificial intelligence models.

While the Bartz ruling previously found that using books to train large language models constituted fair use, it blocked the creation of a permanent central library using pirated files. The plaintiffs in Cruz v. Anthropic are seeking statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, significantly higher than the payout provided under the class-action settlement.

entry.title: Silicon Valley AI Political Factions Divide Over 2026 Midterm Spending Strategy
entry.content:
Links: cnbc.com

Political action committees and super PACs backed by Silicon Valley tech heavyweights have divided into competing factions over regulatory strategy in the 2026 congressional midterms. Groups advocating for rapid AI innovation and uniform federal rules have spent approximately $8 million in general-election races, outspending rival factions pushing for strict safety guardrails and state-level authority, which have deployed roughly $6.9 million according to Federal Election Commission data.

Modeled after cryptocurrency industry spending, initial efforts sought to build a unified political machine, but intense infighting and high-profile clashes—such as a $23 million primary battle in New York—have triggered voter backlash. Consequently, overall spending slowed sharply heading into November, with major backers scaling back their contributions amid mounting reputational risks and public skepticism toward unhindered AI expansion.

entry.title: Missileer Watch Tracks Military Emergency Action Messages on Shortwave Radio
entry.content:
Links: missileer.watch | hacker news

Missileer Watch is an online platform that provides a live shortwave radio feed and historical archive of United States military Emergency Action Messages broadcast over the High Frequency Global Communications System on 11175 kHz. The site makes intercepted tactical broadcasts accessible to the public alongside crowd-corrected transcripts and aircraft tracking data.

Developed by former 321st Missile Squadron combat crew member Daniel Frenkel, the project offers transparency into military communication channels without compromising operational security, as the underlying tactical messages remain heavily encrypted. Operating with minimal tracking and open-source licensing, the platform serves as a resource for radio enthusiasts and researchers monitoring strategic command traffic.

entry.title: Privacy Risks of Sensitive Data in Application Log Files
entry.content:
Links: fireborn.mataroa.blog | discussion

Log files attached to software support requests and bug reports frequently contain unintended sensitive information, including screen text, private messages, account identifiers, and authentication tokens. Because applications often log extensive internal state and user interactions during debugging, diagnostic files can inadvertently expose confidential personal data.

Users are advised to treat diagnostic warnings seriously and avoid blindly sharing unfiltered log archives when reporting bugs. At the same time, software developers bear responsibility for adopting safe defaults—such as keeping diagnostic logging disabled by default—and implementing selective logging to minimize privacy risks.

entry.title: Canadian Bill C-22 Lawful Access Legislation Faces Opposition in Senate
entry.content:
Links: eff.org | hacker news

Canada’s Parliament is advancing Bill C-22, also known as the Lawful Access Act, which has passed the House of Commons and is currently before the Senate. The legislation would grant the government sweeping powers to mandate surveillance features, require telecommunications companies and messaging apps to retain user metadata for up to a year, and potentially compromise encryption by allowing backdoor access for law enforcement.

Civil liberties groups, including the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and Citizen Lab, have criticized the bill for severe constitutional, cybersecurity, and cross-border data-sharing risks. Critics warn that the measure could allow foreign law enforcement agencies, such as those in the United States, to access Canadian user data without domestic court oversight, prompting intense pushback from privacy advocates and the technology sector.

entry.content:

The mandate affects all applications, including those distributed via alternative open-source platforms like F-Droid or sideloaded independently, by introducing mandatory identity checks and cryptographic signing verification.
